title: Die weiße und die schwarze Braut
titleEn: The White Bride and the Black Bride
part: The White Bride and the Black Bride
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 135. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly (daß, anthun, thun, güldene, geschahs).
about: KHM 135 runs on a stark opposition: white and black stand for blessing and curse, kindness and spite, the true bride and the false one put in her place. A mother turns away God disguised as a beggar and is struck coal-black and ugly on the spot along with her own daughter, while the kind stepdaughter is made white and fair; later the black daughter and her mother connive to drown the fair bride and pass off the substitute to a king, undone only when the drowned girl returns as a white duck asking after her enchanted brother. It is one of the collection's plainer moral geometries, and the tale states it without hedging.
advisory: In this tale black skin is a curse from God and white skin a blessing, and the villain is called “the black one” from then on.

sentences.t: Eine Frau gieng mit ihrer Tochter und Stieftochter über Feld, Futter zu schneiden.
sentences.l: A woman went with her daughter and step-daughter over field, to cut fodder.
sentences.i: A woman went out across the fields with her daughter and her step-daughter, to cut fodder.
sentences.n: gieng is the 1857 spelling of ging, and the tale keeps the old forms throughout — gieng, hieng, thun/that, Schooß, heirathete. “über Feld gehen” is to go out across open country. Futter is fodder cut green for the beasts: the errand of a poor household.

sentences.t: Da kam der liebe Gott als ein armer Mann zu ihnen gegangen und fragte „wo führt der Weg ins Dorf?“
sentences.l: There came the dear God to them as a poor man, walking, and asked “where does the way lead into the village?”
sentences.i: Then the dear Lord came walking up to them as a poor man, and asked: “Where does the road lead to the village?”
sentences.n: “kam … gegangen” is a turn English has no copy for: the participle says how he came — came walking. der liebe Gott, the dear God, is the ordinary German name for God in these tales and is kept as such. He walks the earth in poor clothes and tests whoever he meets, exactly as in KHM 87.

sentences.t: „Wenn ihr ihn wissen wollt,“ sprach die Mutter, „so sucht ihn selber,“
sentences.l: “If you want to know it,” spoke the mother, “then look for it yourself,”
sentences.i: “If you want to know it,” said the mother, “then find it yourself,”
sentences.n: ihn is the way, der Weg — masculine, so German says “him” where English says “it.” The mother uses ihr, the plural you, to a stranger: polite in form, contemptuous in tone here. sprach is the tale-teller’s word for “said” and will come on nearly every line.

sentences.t: und die Tochter setzte hinzu „habt ihr Sorge daß ihr ihn nicht findet, so nehmt euch einen Wegweiser mit.“
sentences.l: and the daughter added “if you have care that you will not find it, then take a signpost along with you.”
sentences.i: and the daughter added: “If you are afraid you will not find it, take a signpost along with you.”
sentences.n: “setzte hinzu” is hinzusetzen, to add, with hinzu at the end. “Sorge haben daß …” is to be afraid that. The mockery is heavy-footed: a Wegweiser is a fingerpost planted at a crossroads, and nobody carries one about. Two refusals, and the tale has said all it needs about the pair.

sentences.t: Die Stieftochter aber sprach „armer Mann, ich will dich führen, komm mit mir.“
sentences.l: The step-daughter however said “poor man, I will lead you, come with me.”
sentences.i: But the step-daughter said: “Poor man, I will guide you — come with me.”
sentences.n: She says du to him where the other two said ihr: the familiar form, which to a beggar is not rudeness but nearness. aber standing in second place — “Die Stieftochter aber” — marks the turn: but she.

sentences.t: Da zürnte der liebe Gott über die Mutter und Tochter, wendete ihnen den Rücken zu und verwünschte sie, daß sie sollten schwarz werden wie die Nacht und häßlich wie die Sünde.
sentences.l: Then the dear God was angry over the mother and daughter, turned his back to them and cursed them, that they should become black as the night and ugly as sin.
sentences.i: Then the dear Lord grew angry with the mother and the daughter, turned his back on them and cursed them, that they should become black as night and ugly as sin.
sentences.n: “wendete ihnen den Rücken zu” is zuwenden with the prefix at the end, and the dative ihnen says to whom. The curse — schwarz wie die Nacht und häßlich wie die Sünde — sets up the colour opposition that runs the whole tale: from here the stepsister is die Schwarze, the black one, and the heroine die Weiße, the white one. Black for the wicked and white for the good is the tale’s moral machinery, stated in these words by the German and left in these words in the English.

sentences.t: Der armen Stieftochter aber war Gott gnädig und gieng mit ihr,
sentences.l: To the poor step-daughter however God was gracious and went with her,
sentences.i: But to the poor step-daughter God was gracious, and he went with her,
sentences.n: “jemandem gnädig sein” takes the dative — der armen Stieftochter — and that dative stands first in the sentence, which German may do and English can only shadow.

sentences.t: und als sie nahe am Dorf waren, sprach er einen Segen über sie und sagte „wähle dir drei Sachen aus, die will ich dir gewähren.“
sentences.l: and when they were near the village, he spoke a blessing over her and said “choose out three things for yourself, these will I grant you.”
sentences.i: and when they were near the village, he spoke a blessing over her and said: “Choose three things for yourself, and I will grant them to you.”
sentences.n: “wähle … aus” is auswählen, with aus waiting at the end; dir is the dative of advantage — choose for yourself. Three wishes granted by a stranger met on the road is one of the oldest shapes in the collection, and the third wish is always the test.

sentences.t: Da sprach das Mädchen „ich möchte gern so schön und rein werden wie die Sonne;“
sentences.l: Then the girl said “I should like to become as fair and pure as the sun;”
sentences.n: “möchte gern” is the polite wish-form, I should like. rein is pure and clean at once — of the skin as well as of the soul, and the tale means both.

sentences.t: alsbald war sie weiß und schön wie der Tag.
sentences.l: at once she was white and fair as the day.
sentences.i: and at once she was white and fair as the day.
sentences.n: alsbald, straightway — already an old word in 1857. She wished to be like the sun and is granted “white and fair as the day”: the tale is fixing its two poles, day against the night of the curse.

sentences.t: „Dann möchte ich einen Geldbeutel haben, der nie leer würde:“
sentences.l: “Then I should like to have a purse that would never become empty:”
sentences.i: “Then I should like a purse that never grew empty:”
sentences.n: würde is the subjunctive of the thing wished for — a purse that never *would* run empty, since it does not exist yet. A Geldbeutel is the money-bag carried at the belt.

sentences.t: den gab ihr der liebe Gott auch, sprach aber „vergiß das Beste nicht.“
sentences.l: that the dear God gave her too, but said “do not forget the best.”
sentences.i: That too the dear Lord gave her, but he said: “Do not forget the best.”
sentences.n: den stands first, picking up the purse from the sentence before: German puts the object in front whenever it likes, and the verb still comes second. The warning is the hinge — two wishes have gone on this world.

sentences.t: Sagte sie „ich wünsche mir zum dritten das ewige Himmelreich nach meinem Tode.“
sentences.l: Said she “I wish myself for the third the eternal kingdom of heaven after my death.”
sentences.i: She said: “For the third I wish for the everlasting kingdom of heaven after my death.”
sentences.n: The verb comes first with no subject before it — Sagte sie — which hurries the telling along. “zum dritten,” as the third; “sich etwas wünschen” puts the wisher in the dative, mir.

sentences.t: Das ward ihr auch gewährt, und also schied der liebe Gott von ihr.
sentences.l: That was granted her too, and so the dear God parted from her.
sentences.i: That was granted her too, and so the dear Lord parted from her.
sentences.n: ward is the old past of werden, here the passive auxiliary: es ward gewährt, it was granted. also here is “thus, so,” not the modern also; “scheiden von” is to part from.

sentences.t: Als die Stiefmutter mit ihrer Tochter nach Hause kam und sah daß sie beide kohlschwarz und häßlich waren, die Stieftochter aber weiß und schön,
sentences.l: When the stepmother came home with her daughter and saw that the two of them were coal-black and ugly, but the step-daughter white and fair,
sentences.i: When the stepmother came home with her daughter and saw that they were both coal-black and ugly, while the step-daughter was white and fair,
sentences.n: daß with ß is the 1857 spelling of dass. kohlschwarz, coal-black, is the everyday intensive, as English says jet-black. German can hold its main clause back for as long as it likes, and here it holds it into the next sentence-unit.

sentences.t: so stieg die Bosheit in ihrem Herzen noch höher, und sie hatte nichts anders im Sinn als wie sie ihr ein Leid anthun könnte.
sentences.l: then the malice rose in her heart still higher, and she had nothing else in mind than how she might do her a harm.
sentences.i: the malice in her heart rose higher still, and she had nothing else in mind but how she might do her some harm.
sentences.n: so opens the main clause after the long when-clause: German marks the resumption this way and English simply drops it. “ein Leid anthun” = jemandem ein Leid antun, to do somebody a harm — anthun is the 1857 spelling of antun, prefix at the end. Bosheit is malice, not mere naughtiness.

sentences.t: Die Stieftochter aber hatte einen Bruder Namens Reginer, den liebte sie sehr und erzählte ihm alles, was geschehen war.
sentences.l: The step-daughter however had a brother by name Reginer, him she loved very much and told him everything that had happened.
sentences.i: But the step-daughter had a brother named Reginer, whom she loved dearly, and she told him everything that had happened.
sentences.n: Namens is a bare genitive, “by name.” den at the head of the clause is the object put in front and taken up by the verb — “den liebte sie sehr,” him she loved dearly — a construction the tales use constantly. Reginer is left as it stands; it is an old Germanic name, the Regin- of Reginald.

sentences.t: Nun sprach Reginer einmal zu ihr „liebe Schwester, ich will dich abmalen, damit ich dich beständig vor Augen sehe, denn meine Liebe zu dir ist so groß, daß ich dich immer anblicken möchte.“
sentences.l: Now Reginer said to her one day “dear sister, I will paint you, so that I may see you constantly before my eyes, for my love for you is so great that I should like to look at you always.”
sentences.i: Now Reginer said to her one day: “Dear sister, I will paint your likeness, so that I may have you always before my eyes; for my love for you is so great that I would look at you for ever.”
sentences.n: abmalen is to paint someone’s likeness — ab- because the picture is taken off the living face. damit opens a purpose clause, denn gives a reason. The brother’s love is stated at this length because the tale needs it to explain everything he does afterwards.

sentences.t: Da antwortete sie „aber ich bitte dich laß niemand das Bild sehen.“
sentences.l: Then she answered “but I beg you, let nobody see the picture.”
sentences.n: “laß … sehen” is lassen with a bare infinitive, to let someone see. Her one condition — and everything that follows comes of its being broken, though it is broken by the court and not by him.

sentences.t: Er malte nun seine Schwester ab und hieng das Bild in seiner Stube auf;
sentences.l: He now painted his sister off and hung the picture up in his room;
sentences.i: So he painted his sister’s likeness and hung the picture up in his room;
sentences.n: Both verbs are separable and both prefixes wait at the end: malte … ab, hieng … auf. hieng is the 1857 spelling of hing. A Stube is the living-room — in a small dwelling, the one heated room.

sentences.t: er wohnte aber in des Königs Schloß, weil er bei ihm Kutscher war.
sentences.l: he lived however in the king’s castle, because he was coachman with him.
sentences.i: but he lived in the king’s castle, for he was coachman to the king.
sentences.n: “des Königs Schloß” is the old genitive standing in front of its noun, which German now mostly avoids. “bei ihm Kutscher sein” — bei carries the employment: in his service as coachman.

sentences.t: Alle Tage gieng er davor stehen und dankte Gott für das Glück seiner lieben Schwester.
sentences.l: Every day he went to stand before it and thanked God for the good fortune of his dear sister.
sentences.i: Every day he would go and stand before it and thank God for his dear sister’s good fortune.
sentences.n: “Alle Tage” is an accusative of time. “gieng … stehen” is gehen with a bare infinitive: went and stood. davor, before it — before the picture.

sentences.t: Nun war aber gerade dem König, bei dem er diente, seine Gemahlin verstorben,
sentences.l: Now however to the king, with whom he served, his consort had died,
sentences.i: Now it happened that the king he served had just lost his wife,
sentences.n: The dative dem König with a possessive after it — to the king … his consort — is the dative of possession, and it is how German most naturally says whose wife died. Gemahlin is the elevated word for a wife of rank; versterben is the formal word for dying.

sentences.t: und die so schön gewesen war, daß man keine finden konnte, die ihr gliche,
sentences.l: and she had been so beautiful that one could find none who resembled her,
sentences.i: and she had been so beautiful that none could be found to match her,
sentences.n: gliche is the subjunctive after a negative: none who *would* resemble her. gleichen takes the dative, ihr. A dead queen no one can match is exactly what makes the picture dangerous.

sentences.t: und der König war darüber in tiefer Trauer.
sentences.l: and the king was over that in deep mourning.
sentences.i: and the king was in deep mourning for her.
sentences.n: darüber, over that, points back to the whole death. Trauer is both the grief and the outward mourning, the black clothes — the tale is already dressing its stage in black and white.

sentences.t: Die Hofdiener bemerkten aber daß der Kutscher täglich vor dem schönen Bilde stand, mißgönntens ihm und meldeten es dem König.
sentences.l: The court servants however noticed that the coachman stood daily before the beautiful picture, begrudged it him and reported it to the king.
sentences.i: But the court servants noticed that the coachman stood every day before the beautiful picture; they begrudged it him and reported it to the king.
sentences.n: mißgönntens is mißgönnten es with the es swallowed into the verb, as speech swallows it; the printed text keeps the spoken form. mißgönnen is to begrudge someone the good thing he has, and takes the dative of the person, ihm. Bilde carries the old dative -e.

sentences.t: Da ließ dieser das Bild vor sich bringen, und als er sah daß es in allem seiner verstorbenen Frau glich, nur noch schöner war, so verliebte er sich sterblich hinein.
sentences.l: Then he had the picture brought before him, and when he saw that it in everything resembled his dead wife, only was still more beautiful, so he fell mortally in love with it.
sentences.i: So the king had the picture brought before him; and when he saw that it was his dead wife in every particular, only more beautiful still, he fell mortally in love with it.
sentences.n: dieser, “the latter,” points back to the king and not to the servants. “ließ … bringen” is lassen with an infinitive, to have a thing done. “sich verlieben in” takes the accusative, and hinein carries it: he falls in love *into* the picture. sterblich, mortally, is the tale’s own word.

sentences.t: Er ließ den Kutscher vor sich kommen und fragte wen das Bild vorstellte.
sentences.l: He had the coachman come before him and asked whom the picture represented.
sentences.i: He had the coachman brought before him and asked whom the picture showed.
sentences.n: vorstellen here is to represent, to depict — not to introduce, which is what it usually means now.

sentences.t: Der Kutscher sagte es wäre seine Schwester,
sentences.l: The coachman said it was his sister,
sentences.n: wäre is the subjunctive of reported speech: the tale gives his words without vouching for them, which German marks with the subjunctive where English changes at most a tense.

sentences.t: so entschloß sich der König keine andere als diese zur Gemahlin zu nehmen,
sentences.l: so the king resolved to take no other than this one as his consort,
sentences.i: so the king resolved to take no other than her to wife,
sentences.n: “sich entschließen,” to resolve. “zur Gemahlin nehmen” is the set phrase for taking someone to wife — zu with the dative of what she is to become.

sentences.t: gab ihm Wagen und Pferde und prächtige Goldkleider und schickte ihn fort, seine erwählte Braut abzuholen.
sentences.l: gave him carriage and horses and splendid golden clothes and sent him off, to fetch his chosen bride.
sentences.n: The subject is still the king, four verbs on — German strings them without repeating him. Goldkleider, cloth-of-gold clothes, will matter twice more: they are what the black bride is wearing when she is taken for the white one. erwählt is chosen, elected, a formal word.

sentences.t: Wie Reginer mit der Botschaft an kam, freute sich seine Schwester,
sentences.l: When Reginer arrived with the message, his sister rejoiced,
sentences.i: When Reginer came with the message, his sister rejoiced,
sentences.n: Wie here is “when,” as it often is in these tales. The source prints “an kam” as two words where modern German writes ankam — the old printer’s habit with separable verbs, left as it stands.

sentences.t: allein die Schwarze war eifersüchtig über das Glück, ärgerte sich über alle Maßen
sentences.l: but the black one was jealous over the good fortune, was vexed beyond all measure
sentences.i: but the black one was jealous of her good fortune, and was vexed beyond all measure
sentences.n: allein here is the conjunction “but,” not the adjective “alone.” die Schwarze is an adjective used as a noun — the black one, the black woman — and from here the tale names the two sisters by their colours only: die Schwarze and die Weiße. “über alle Maßen,” beyond all measure, with the old plural Maßen.

sentences.t: und sprach zu ihrer Mutter „was helfen nun all eure Künste, da ihr mir ein solches Glück doch nicht verschaffen könnt.“
sentences.l: and said to her mother “what use are all your arts now, since you cannot get me such good fortune after all.”
sentences.i: and said to her mother: “What use are all your arts now, since for all of them you cannot get me such good fortune.”
sentences.n: Künste are the witch’s arts. The daughter says ihr, the plural you, to her own mother — the respectful form a child used to a parent well into the last century. doch carries the reproach: for all of them, you cannot.

sentences.t: „Sei still,“ sagte die Alte „ich will dirs schon zuwenden.“
sentences.l: “Be still,” said the old woman, “I will turn it your way yet.”
sentences.i: “Be quiet,” said the old woman; “I shall turn it your way yet.”
sentences.n: die Alte, the old one, is the tale’s name for the stepmother from here on. dirs is dir es, contracted. zuwenden is to turn something toward someone, with the dative of the person; schon here is not “already” but the particle of assurance — never fear, I shall manage it.

sentences.t: Und durch ihre Hexenkünste trübte sie dem Kutscher die Augen, daß er halb blind war,
sentences.l: And through her witch-arts she clouded the coachman’s eyes, so that he was half blind,
sentences.i: And by her witchcraft she clouded the coachman’s eyes, so that he was half blind,
sentences.n: “trübte sie dem Kutscher die Augen” — the dative of possession again: whose eyes is said with a dative and not a possessive. trüben is to make cloudy, to dim. Everything that follows rests on these two mutilations, his eyes and her ears.

sentences.t: und der Weißen verstopfte sie die Ohren, daß sie halb taub war.
sentences.l: and the white one’s ears she stopped up, so that she was half deaf.
sentences.i: and she stopped the white one’s ears, so that she was half deaf.
sentences.n: der Weißen is the dative of die Weiße, the white one — the same adjective-as-noun as die Schwarze, and now the pair is complete. verstopfen is to stop up, to plug.

sentences.t: Darauf stiegen sie in den Wagen, erst die Braut in den herrlichen königlichen Kleidern, dann die Stiefmutter mit ihrer Tochter,
sentences.l: Thereupon they climbed into the carriage, first the bride in the splendid royal clothes, then the stepmother with her daughter,
sentences.i: Thereupon they got into the carriage: first the bride in her splendid royal clothes, then the stepmother with her daughter,
sentences.n: Darauf, thereupon. The order of seating is given because the order is what matters: the bride is shut inside with the two who mean to destroy her.

sentences.t: und Reginer saß auf dem Bock, um zu fahren.
sentences.l: and Reginer sat on the box, in order to drive.
sentences.i: and Reginer sat on the box to drive.
sentences.n: The Bock is the coachman’s seat on the front of a carriage, high up and facing forward — which is why he can call back to his sister but cannot see what is done to her. “um zu” with an infinitive is the purpose construction.

sentences.t: Wie sie eine Weile unterwegs waren, rief der Kutscher
sentences.l: When they had been a while on the way, the coachman called
sentences.i: When they had been a while on the road, the coachman called:
sentences.n: Wie again for “when”; unterwegs, on the way. What follows is the first of his three rhymed calls.

sentences.t:
„deck dich zu, mein Schwesterlein,
daß Regen dich nicht näßt,
daß Wind dich nicht bestäubt
daß du fein schön zum König kommst.“
sentences.l:
“Cover yourself up, my little sister,
that rain does not wet you,
that wind does not powder you with dust
that you come fine and fair to the king.”
sentences.i:
“Cover yourself up, my little sister,
so the rain does not wet you,
so the wind does not powder you with dust,
so you come to the king fine and fair.”
sentences.n: The brother’s call from the box, which comes twice more with small changes. The German runs on a beat rather than a strict rhyme: näßt and bestäubt chime without rhyming exactly, and Schwesterlein carries the ear. Lectorium’s idiomatic line does not rhyme — it renders the sense plainly. “deck dich zu” is zudecken, to cover up, with zu at the end; Schwesterlein is the tender diminutive. This first call has no comma after bestäubt and no und before the last line; the two later calls add both.

sentences.t: Die Braut fragte „was sagt mein lieber Bruder?“
sentences.l: The bride asked “what does my dear brother say?”
sentences.n: She has to ask because her ears are stopped: the witchcraft has made her depend on the one person who means to ruin her. This exchange comes three times, almost word for word.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ sprach die Alte, „er hat gesagt du solltest dein gülden Kleid ausziehen und es deiner Schwester geben.“
sentences.l: “Ah,” said the old woman, “he has said you should take off your golden dress and give it to your sister.”
sentences.i: “Ah,” said the old woman, “he said you should take off your golden dress and give it to your sister.”
sentences.n: gülden is the old form of golden, here uninflected before Kleid — dein gülden Kleid, as an older German said it. solltest is the subjunctive of reported speech: what he is supposed to have said. The lie is of the simplest kind, since the brother said nothing of the sort.

sentences.t: Da zog sies aus und thats der Schwarzen an, die gab ihr dafür einen schlechten grauen Kittel.
sentences.l: Then she took it off and put it on the black one; that one gave her a poor grey smock for it in return.
sentences.i: So she took it off and put it on the black one, who gave her a poor grey smock in return.
sentences.n: sies is sie es and thats is that es, both swallowed as speech swallows them. “zog … aus” and “that … an” are ausziehen and anthun, the old pair for taking clothes off and putting them on. schlecht here has its older sense of plain, poor in quality, not morally bad; a Kittel is a coarse working smock.

sentences.t: So fuhren sie weiter: über ein Weilchen rief der Bruder abermals
sentences.l: So they drove on further: after a little while the brother called again
sentences.i: So they drove on; and after a little while the brother called again:
sentences.n: “über ein Weilchen,” after a little while — über of elapsed time. abermals, once again, is an old word; Weilchen is the diminutive of Weile.

sentences.t:
„deck dich zu, mein Schwesterlein,
daß Regen dich nicht näßt,
daß Wind dich nicht bestäubt,
und du fein schön zum König kommst.“
sentences.l:
“Cover yourself up, my little sister,
that rain does not wet you,
that wind does not powder you with dust,
and you come fine and fair to the king.”
sentences.i:
“Cover yourself up, my little sister,
so the rain does not wet you,
so the wind does not powder you with dust,
and you come to the king fine and fair.”
sentences.n: The same call, with two small changes from the first: a comma after bestäubt and und before the last line. The variation is the point — he says it three times, and each time his sister is stripped of something more.

sentences.t: Die Braut fragte „was sagt mein lieber Bruder?“
sentences.l: The bride asked “what does my dear brother say?”
sentences.n: The same question, and the same helplessness behind it.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ sprach die Alte, „er hat gesagt, du solltest deine güldene Haube ab thun und deiner Schwester geben.“
sentences.l: “Ah,” said the old woman, “he has said you should take off your golden cap and give it to your sister.”
sentences.i: “Ah,” said the old woman, “he said you should take off your golden cap and give it to your sister.”
sentences.n: güldene is inflected here where the first lie had the bare gülden. A Haube is the close cap a betrothed or married woman wore, and a golden one belongs to the bridal dress — so the second theft takes her standing as well as her finery. “ab thun” is abthun (modern abtun), printed as two words.

sentences.t: Da that sie die Haube ab und that sie der Schwarzen auf und saß im bloßen Haar.
sentences.l: Then she took the cap off and put it on the black one, and sat in her bare hair.
sentences.i: So she took off the cap and set it on the black one, and sat there bare-headed.
sentences.n: that … ab and that … auf: the same verb thun with two prefixes, one after the other. “im bloßen Haar” is to sit with nothing but one’s hair — bare-headed, which for a bride on her way to a king is a public shame, and that is what the old woman wanted.

sentences.t: So fuhren sie weiter: wiederum über ein Weilchen rief der Bruder
sentences.l: So they drove on further: again after a little while the brother called
sentences.i: So they drove on; and again after a little while the brother called:
sentences.n: wiederum, once more. The third round is announced in almost the words of the second: the pattern is fixed, and the reader is meant to feel it tightening.

sentences.t:
„deck dich zu, mein Schwesterlein,
daß Regen dich nicht näßt,
daß Wind dich nicht bestäubt,
und du fein schön zum König kommst.“
sentences.l:
“Cover yourself up, my little sister,
that rain does not wet you,
that wind does not powder you with dust,
and you come fine and fair to the king.”
sentences.i:
“Cover yourself up, my little sister,
so the rain does not wet you,
so the wind does not powder you with dust,
and you come to the king fine and fair.”
sentences.n: The third call, word for word as the second. It is the last thing he says to her from the box, and the next lie will cost her her life.

sentences.t: Die Braut fragte „was sagt mein lieber Bruder?“
sentences.l: The bride asked “what does my dear brother say?”
sentences.n: The third asking, word for word as the other two.

sentences.t: „Ach,“ sprach die Alte, „er hat gesagt du möchtest einmal aus dem Wagen sehen.“
sentences.l: “Ah,” said the old woman, “he has said you might look out of the carriage once.”
sentences.i: “Ah,” said the old woman, “he said you should look out of the carriage a moment.”
sentences.n: möchtest is the subjunctive again, the polite form of a request in reported speech: that you would look out. The first two lies took her clothes; this one takes her life.

sentences.t: Sie fuhren aber gerade auf einer Brücke über ein tiefes Wasser.
sentences.l: They were driving however just then on a bridge over a deep water.
sentences.i: But they were just then driving over a bridge above deep water.
sentences.n: gerade, just at that moment. The tale hands the reader the bridge one sentence before it is used — which is how a told tale prepares its shock.

sentences.t: Wie nun die Braut aufstand und aus dem Wagen sich heraus bückte, da stießen sie die beiden hinaus, daß sie mitten ins Wasser stürzte.
sentences.l: When now the bride stood up and bent herself out of the carriage, then the two of them pushed her out, so that she plunged right into the middle of the water.
sentences.i: And when the bride stood up and leaned out of the carriage, the two of them pushed her out, so that she plunged into the middle of the water.
sentences.n: “sich heraus bücken,” to bend out, and “stießen … hinaus,” hinausstoßen, to push out — both prefixes at the end, both pointing away from the speaker. die beiden, the two of them: mother and daughter act together. The tale states the murder and passes no comment on it.

sentences.t: Als sie versunken war, in demselben Augenblick, stieg eine schneeweiße Ente aus dem Wasserspiegel hervor und schwamm den Fluß hinab.
sentences.l: When she had sunk, in the same moment, a snow-white duck rose up out of the water’s surface and swam away down the river.
sentences.i: When she had sunk, in that same moment a snow-white duck rose from the surface of the water and swam away down the river.
sentences.n: Wasserspiegel is the water-mirror, the surface. “stieg … hervor,” hervorsteigen, to come up out of; “schwamm den Fluß hinab” puts the way travelled in the accusative. The change is given no explanation whatever: the murdered girl simply is a duck, and snow-white, which is her colour.

sentences.t: Der Bruder hatte gar nichts davon gemerkt und fuhr den Wagen weiter, bis sie an den Hof kamen.
sentences.l: The brother had noticed nothing at all of it and drove the carriage on until they came to the court.
sentences.i: The brother had noticed nothing of it at all, and drove on until they came to the court.
sentences.n: “gar nichts,” nothing whatever; davon, of it. Hof here is the royal court, the household — not a farmyard.

sentences.t: Da brachte er dem König die Schwarze als seine Schwester und meinte sie wärs wirklich,
sentences.l: Then he brought the black one to the king as his sister and thought she really was the one,
sentences.i: So he brought the black one to the king as his sister, believing that she really was,
sentences.n: wärs is wäre es, and the wäre is the subjunctive of what he supposed. meinen here is to be of the opinion, to suppose — not to mean.

sentences.t: weil es ihm trübe vor den Augen war und er doch die Goldkleider schimmern sah.
sentences.l: because it was dim before his eyes and he did after all see the golden clothes shimmering.
sentences.i: because his sight was dim, and he could still see the golden clothes shimmering.
sentences.n: “es war ihm trübe vor den Augen” is impersonal, with the person in the dative: things were dim before his eyes. The stolen golden clothes do the rest — he knows his sister by her dress, which is precisely why the old woman took it.

sentences.t: Der König, wie er die grundlose Häßlichkeit an seiner vermeinten Braut erblickte,
sentences.l: The king, when he caught sight of the bottomless ugliness in his supposed bride,
sentences.i: The king, when he caught sight of the fathomless ugliness of his supposed bride,
sentences.n: grundlos is literally bottomless — ugliness with no floor to it. vermeint is supposed, presumed; erblicken, to catch sight of, is a stronger word than sehen.

sentences.t: ward sehr bös und befahl den Kutscher in eine Grube zu werfen, die voll Ottern und Schlangengezücht war.
sentences.l: became very angry and commanded the coachman to be thrown into a pit that was full of adders and snake-brood.
sentences.i: grew very angry, and ordered the coachman thrown into a pit that was full of adders and crawling snakes.
sentences.n: ward is the old past of werden. “befahl … zu werfen” gives the order in an infinitive with nobody named to carry it out, so English has to make it passive. Schlangengezücht is a collective in Ge-: the whole brood or spawn of snakes, a word of disgust. The punishment falls on the one innocent man in the carriage, and the tale enters no protest.

sentences.t: Die alte Hexe aber wußte den König doch so zu bestricken und durch ihre Künste ihm die Augen zu verblenden,
sentences.l: The old witch however knew how so to ensnare the king and by her arts to blind his eyes,
sentences.i: But the old witch knew how to ensnare the king so, and to blind his eyes by her arts,
sentences.n: “wissen zu” with an infinitive is to know how to do a thing, and here it carries a whole plot in one verb. bestricken is literally to net or snare, from Strick, a cord; verblenden is to blind or dazzle so that one cannot judge, with the dative ihm for whose eyes.

sentences.t: daß er sie und ihre Tochter behielt, ja daß sie ihm ganz leidlich vorkam und er sich wirklich mit ihr verheirathete.
sentences.l: that he kept her and her daughter, indeed that she seemed to him quite tolerable and he really married her.
sentences.i: that he kept her and her daughter — indeed, that the girl seemed to him quite tolerable, and he really married her.
sentences.n: ja here is “indeed, what is more,” raising the stake. “jemandem vorkommen,” to seem to someone, with the dative ihm; leidlich is tolerable, passable. heirathete is the 1857 spelling of heiratete. The tale lets the wicked keep their winnings for a good while and is in no hurry to undo them.

sentences.t: Einmal Abends, während die schwarze Braut dem König auf dem Schooße saß,
sentences.l: One evening, while the black bride sat on the king’s lap,
sentences.i: One evening, while the black bride was sitting on the king’s lap,
sentences.n: “Einmal Abends” is an old adverbial genitive: one evening. Schooße is the 1857 spelling of Schoße, the lap, and dem König is once more the dative of possession — whose lap.

sentences.t: kam eine weiße Ente zum Gossenstein in die Küche geschwommen und sagte zum Küchenjungen
sentences.l: a white duck came swimming through the gutter-stone into the kitchen and said to the kitchen-boy
sentences.i: a white duck came swimming in through the drain into the kitchen and said to the kitchen-boy:
sentences.n: “kam … geschwommen” is the same turn as “kam … gegangen” in the first paragraph: the participle says how she came. A Gossenstein is the stone drain-hole in the kitchen wall through which the slops ran out — the duck’s way in and out, and the lowest opening in her own house.

sentences.t:
„Jüngelchen, mach Feuer an,
daß ich meine Federn wärmen kann.“
sentences.l:
“Little lad, make a fire,
that I may warm my feathers.”
sentences.i:
“Little lad, light a fire,
so that I can warm my feathers.”
sentences.n: The duck speaks in rhyme where the tale speaks in prose — an with kann. Jüngelchen is a diminutive of Junge, little lad; “mach … an” is anmachen, to light, with the prefix at the end.

sentences.t: Das that der Küchenjunge und machte ihr ein Feuer auf dem Herd:
sentences.l: That the kitchen-boy did, and made her a fire on the hearth:
sentences.i: The kitchen-boy did so, and made her a fire on the hearth;
sentences.n: Das stands first — that he did — the object put in front because the sentence before has set it up. ihr, for her: the dative of advantage.

sentences.t: da kam die Ente und setzte sich daneben, schüttelte sich und strich sich die Federn mit dem Schnabel zurecht.
sentences.l: then the duck came and set herself down beside it, shook herself and stroked her feathers straight with her beak.
sentences.i: and the duck came and settled beside it, shook herself, and preened her feathers straight with her beak.
sentences.n: Three reflexives in a row — setzte sich, schüttelte sich, strich sich — where English keeps one and drops the rest. “zurecht streichen” is to stroke into order, to preen, with zurecht at the end. For one sentence the tale simply watches a duck by a fire.

sentences.t: Während sie so saß und sich wohlthat, fragte sie
sentences.l: While she sat so and did herself good, she asked
sentences.i: While she sat there taking her ease, she asked:
sentences.n: “sich wohlthun” (modern wohltun) is to do oneself good, to take one’s ease — the fire is the first kindness she has had since the bridge.

sentences.t: „was macht mein Bruder Reginer?“
sentences.l: “what is my brother Reginer doing?”
sentences.n: The first of the duck’s two questions, asked three nights running. This one line stands as its own verse block in the 1857 text, set off from the prose around it.

sentences.t: Der Küchenjunge antwortete
sentences.l: The kitchen-boy answered
sentences.n: The plainest possible tag. The tale has dropped into the shape of a ballad here: question, answer, three nights over.

sentences.t:
„liegt in der Grube gefangen
bei Ottern und bei Schlangen.“
sentences.l:
“[He] lies caught in the pit
among adders and among snakes.”
sentences.i:
“He lies a prisoner in the pit,
among adders and among snakes.”
sentences.n: The kitchen-boy answers in the duck’s own rhyme — gefangen with Schlangen. The subject is left out (er liegt), so I have supplied [He] in square brackets. A Grube is a pit dug in the ground; the Ottern are adders, the Schlangengezücht of the earlier sentence.

sentences.t: Fragte sie weiter
sentences.l: She asked further
sentences.i: Then she asked on:
sentences.n: The verb comes first with no subject in front of it — Fragte sie — which the tales do at moments of speed.

sentences.t: „was macht die schwarze Hexe im Haus?“
sentences.l: “what is the black witch doing in the house?”
sentences.n: die schwarze Hexe: the answer places her in the king’s arm, so this is the black bride, the stepsister, and not her mother — the tale uses “witch” of both women, and names them by the colour of the curse.

sentences.t: Der Küchenjunge antwortete
sentences.l: The kitchen-boy answered
sentences.n: The same tag as before, word for word: the exchange keeps its shape.

sentences.t:
„die sitzt warm
ins Königs Arm.“
sentences.l:
“she sits warm
in the king’s arm.”
sentences.n: warm with Arm is the rhyme. “ins Königs Arm” is an old genitive with the preposition fused to the article — in des Königs Arm — and 1857 prints it as it was spoken.

sentences.t: Sagte die Ente
sentences.l: Said the duck
sentences.n: Verb first once more.

sentences.t: „daß Gott erbarm!“
sentences.l: “that God have mercy!”
sentences.i: “God have mercy!”
sentences.n: Not a sentence but a cry: “daß Gott erbarm” is a set exclamation of pity or outrage, God have mercy on us. erbarm is the old subjunctive of erbarmen without its usual sich, and it rhymes with the Arm of the answer before it.

sentences.t: und schwamm den Gossenstein hinaus.
sentences.l: and swam out through the gutter-stone.
sentences.i: and swam out through the drain.
sentences.n: “den Gossenstein hinaus” puts the way passed through in the accusative — out through the drain. She comes and goes by the slops-hole of what should be her own house.

sentences.t: Den folgenden Abend kam sie wieder und that dieselben Fragen und den dritten Abend noch einmal.
sentences.l: The following evening she came again and did the same questions, and the third evening once more.
sentences.i: The next evening she came again and asked the same questions, and the third evening once more.
sentences.n: “Den folgenden Abend” is an accusative of time. “Fragen thun” — literally to do questions — is the old idiom where modern German says Fragen stellen. Three nights is the folk tale’s measure, and the third is what breaks the case open.

sentences.t: Da konnte es der Küchenjunge nicht länger übers Herz bringen, gieng zu dem König und entdeckte ihm alles.
sentences.l: Then the kitchen-boy could no longer bring it over his heart, went to the king and disclosed everything to him.
sentences.i: Then the kitchen-boy could bear it on his conscience no longer, and went to the king and told him everything.
sentences.n: “es nicht übers Herz bringen” is to be unable to bring oneself to a thing — to find it more than one’s heart will carry. entdecken here is to disclose, to uncover: its older sense, not to discover.

sentences.t: Der König aber wollte es selbst sehen, gieng den andern Abend hin,
sentences.l: The king however wanted to see it himself, went there the next evening,
sentences.i: But the king wanted to see it for himself, and went there the next evening,
sentences.n: “den andern Abend,” the accusative of time again; hin is thither, the direction away from the speaker.

sentences.t: und wie die Ente den Kopf durch den Gossenstein herein streckte, nahm er sein Schwert, und hieb ihr den Hals durch,
sentences.l: and when the duck stretched her head in through the gutter-stone, he took his sword and struck her neck through,
sentences.i: and when the duck put her head in through the drain, he took his sword and struck her neck through,
sentences.n: herein, in toward the speaker, against the hinaus of her leaving. “hieb … durch” is durchhauen, to cut through, with the prefix at the end and the dative ihr for whose neck. Beheading the enchanted duck is, in the logic of the tale, the release and not the murder — though nothing tells the king so before he does it.

sentences.t: da ward sie auf einmal zum schönsten Mädchen und glich genau dem Bild, das der Bruder von ihr gemacht hatte.
sentences.l: then she became at once the most beautiful girl and resembled exactly the picture that the brother had made of her.
sentences.i: and at once she became the most beautiful of girls, and matched exactly the picture her brother had made of her.
sentences.n: “auf einmal,” all at once. “werden zu” with the dative is to turn into something; gleichen again takes the dative, dem Bild. The picture that began the trouble is now the proof of who she is.

sentences.t: Der König war voll Freuden;
sentences.l: The king was full of joys;
sentences.i: The king was full of joy;
sentences.n: Freuden is plural, as German prefers it in this phrase — full of joys.

sentences.t: und weil sie ganz naß da stand, ließ er köstliche Kleider bringen und ließ sie damit bekleiden.
sentences.l: and because she stood there quite wet, he had costly clothes brought and had her clothed with them.
sentences.i: and because she stood there dripping wet, he had costly clothes brought and had her dressed in them.
sentences.n: Two ließ with infinitives in one sentence: the king’s way of doing anything is to have it done. köstlich is costly, precious; bekleiden is the formal word for clothing someone. Grey smock, then bare head, then duck, then wet: the clothes are the last of her restorations.

sentences.t: Dann erzählte sie ihm wie sie durch List und Falschheit wäre betrogen und zuletzt in den Fluß hinabgeworfen worden;
sentences.l: Then she told him how she had been deceived by cunning and falsehood and at last thrown down into the river;
sentences.n: “wäre … betrogen … worden” is the subjunctive passive of reported speech, held across the whole sentence: this is her account, not the tale’s own. List is cunning and Falschheit deceit — the two words the collection keeps for what witches do.

sentences.t: und ihre erste Bitte war, daß ihr Bruder aus der Schlangenhöhle heraus geholt würde.
sentences.l: and her first request was that her brother should be fetched out of the snake-cave.
sentences.i: and her first request was that her brother be fetched out of the snake-pit.
sentences.n: “heraus geholt würde,” the subjunctive of a wish reported. Schlangenhöhle names again the Grube of the earlier sentence. Her first thought on being restored is for the brother who was punished in her place.

sentences.t: Und als der König diese Bitte erfüllt hatte, gieng er in die Kammer, wo die alte Hexe saß und fragte „was verdient die, welche das und das thut?“
sentences.l: And when the king had fulfilled this request, he went into the chamber where the old witch sat and asked “what does she deserve who does such and such?”
sentences.i: And when the king had granted this request, he went into the chamber where the old witch sat, and asked: “What does she deserve who does such and such?”
sentences.n: “das und das” — this and that, such and such: the tale will not repeat the crimes, and the vagueness is what traps her. “die, welche …” is the old relative, she who. Making the guilty pronounce their own sentence is a fixed motif of the collection.

sentences.t: und erzählte was geschehen war.
sentences.l: and told what had happened.
sentences.n: The verb has no subject of its own: it is still the king, four clauses on.

sentences.t: Da war sie so verblendet, daß sie nichts merkte und sprach „die verdient daß man sie nackt auszieht und in ein Faß mit Nägeln legt,
sentences.l: Then she was so blinded that she noticed nothing and said “she deserves that one strip her naked and lay her in a barrel with nails,
sentences.i: But she was so blinded that she noticed nothing, and said: “She deserves to be stripped naked and laid in a barrel stuck with nails,
sentences.n: verblendet, blinded — the word she used on the king, now on herself. man with an active verb is German’s ordinary way of saying what English says with a passive: daß man sie auszieht = that she be stripped. The barrel driven full of nails was a real judicial death, and the tale names it without flinching.

sentences.t: und daß man vor das Faß ein Pferd spannt und das Pferd in alle Welt schickt.“
sentences.l: and that one harness a horse before the barrel and send the horse into all the world.”
sentences.i: and that a horse be harnessed to the barrel and the horse sent out into the wide world.”
sentences.n: “in alle Welt,” into all the world — anywhere and everywhere, until it is finished. She has described her own execution in detail, which is exactly what the king asked her to do.

sentences.t: Das geschah alles an ihr und ihrer schwarzen Tochter.
sentences.l: That all happened to her and to her black daughter.
sentences.i: And all of it was done to her and to her black daughter.
sentences.n: “an jemandem geschehen,” to be done to someone. One flat sentence for the carrying out of what took two to describe — the tale spends more words on the sentence than on the death.

sentences.t: Der König aber heirathete die weiße und schöne Braut und belohnte den treuen Bruder, indem er ihn zu einem reichen und angesehenen Mann machte.
sentences.l: The king however married the white and beautiful bride and rewarded the faithful brother, in that he made him into a rich and respected man.
sentences.i: But the king married the white and beautiful bride, and rewarded the faithful brother by making him a rich and honoured man.
sentences.n: indem with a clause is “by doing so-and-so.” The last sentence sets the two colours against each other one final time — die weiße und schöne Braut here, die schwarze Tochter in the sentence before — which is how the tale has worked since its first paragraph: the colour is the sign of what each is held to deserve.

glossary.allein: allein — but, however (the conjunction; here not the adjective ‘alone’)
glossary.alte: alt — old; here die Alte, the old woman (the tale’s name for the stepmother)
glossary.schlechten: schlecht — poor, plain in quality (adj., inflected; of a garment — the older sense, not morally bad)
glossary.schwarze: schwarz — black (inflected); used as a noun in this tale, ‘die Schwarze’ = the black one, the black bride
glossary.schwarzen: schwarz — black (inflected); as a plain adjective in “ihrer schwarzen Tochter,” and as a noun in “der Schwarzen” = to the black one
glossary.weiße: weiß — white (inflected); used as a noun in this tale, ‘die Weiße’ = the white one, the white bride
glossary.weißen: weiß — white (inflected); as a noun, ‘der Weißen’ = of/to the white one
